Adult Dusky rockfish (Sebastes ciliatus) attain a maximum recorded total length of 53 centimeters [Li = 53 centimeters], a size that places them among the medium-bodied members of the genus in the Gulf of Alaska and adjacent waters. This asymptotic length is typically reached only after many years of relatively slow somatic growth, a pattern common to many long-lived scorpaeniform fishes. The corresponding asymptotic adult wet body mass, derived from the length-weight relationship for this species, is approximately 2100 grams [Wwi = approximately 2100 grams]. Males and females exhibit similar length-at-age trajectories, though females tend to achieve slightly larger ultimate sizes in most surveyed populations, likely reflecting the energetic demands of their viviparous reproductive mode. Field studies employing otolith-based ageing techniques have confirmed that individuals can persist for remarkably long periods; the maximum lifespan observed in wild populations has been documented at approximately 67 years [am = approximately 67 years], with these ancient individuals typically inhabiting the colder, deeper portions of the species' depth range where metabolic deman at a temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]ds are reduced. This exceptional longevity underscores the necessity of cautious management, as populations subject to even moderate fishing pressure may lose their oldest, most fecund individuals, compromising reproductive output over decadal timescales.

Reproductive maturation in Dusky rockfish occurs at a substantially smaller body size than the ultimate maximum. Puberty, defined by the onset of functional gametogenesis in both sexes, is attained when individuals reach a total length of approximately 29 centimeters [Lp = approximately 29 centimeters], which corresponds to a wet body weight at puberty of roughly 330 grams [Wwp = roughly 330 grams]. This size threshold is typically crossed between the ages of five and eight years, depending on local environmental conditions and prey availability. The length at puberty represents roughly 55 percent of the species' asymptotic length, a proportion that is consistent with many other iteroparous marine fishes that exhibit delayed reproduction in favor of continued somatic investment. Females undergo an extended vitellogenic period prior to their first parturition, and the onset of pregnancy places substantial metabolic demands on maturing individuals. The transition from a juvenile, non-reproductive state to a reproductively active adult is therefore a critical life-history bottleneck, one that is particularly sensitive to changes in food supply and water temperature, especially in the high-latitude ecosystems this species inhabits.

The viviparous reproductive strategy of Sebastes ciliatus results in the production of extremely small, free-living larvae following an extended gestation period. At parturition, each newly extruded larva carries a residual yolk mass, and the wet weight of an individual larva at the moment of birth is approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams]. This minute size, equivalent to roughly 0.0008 percent of the weight of an adult female, reflects the optimization of maternal investment across a very large brood: females partition their finite reproductive resources into thousands of tiny offspring rather than a smaller number of large ones. The larvae are immediately planktonic and must rely on endogenous yolk reserves for several days before the onset of exogenous feeding. This initial body mass is among the smallest recorded for any Sebastes species, a trait that constrains the early larval stage to a brief critical period during which suitable prey densities must be encountered. Mortality during these first days is extraordinarily high, and the minuscule larval size imposes tight links between spawning phenology and the spring phytoplankton bloom in subarctic waters.

Reproductive output in Dusky rockfish is strongly influenced by the thermal environment, with metabolic processes governing both gestation duration and the rate of larval development. At a stable water temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C], females have been estimated to produce approximately 800,000 larvae per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 800,000 larvae per spawning event], with a single spawning event occurring each year [F_R_i = single spawning event occurring each year] — a strategy that reflects the species' investment in a single large annual brood rather than multiple smaller clutches. The temperature regime of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C] is typical of the deep-shelf waters this species occupies during its winter spawning season, and metabolic studies suggest that deviations from this thermal optimum would reduce both the number of larvae produced and their individual quality. The longevity of the species, in combination with this high annual output, means that a single female Dusky rockfish can produce hundreds of thousands of larvae over her lifetime, though recruitment to the adult population remains highly variable and density-dependent.

Field records indicate that the maximum lifespan of Sebastes ciliatus reaches 67 years [am = 67 years] when measured under the cold-water conditions characteristic of its preferred habitat at 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]. This extreme longevity is one of the highest documented among the northeastern Pacific rockfishes and is accompanied by a suite of correlated life-history traits: slow growth, late maturation, and low natural adult mortality. Comparative analyses within the genus suggest that the lifespan proxy of 67 years [am = 67 years] is approached only by a handful of other Sebastes species occupying similar cold, deep environments, where reduced metabolic rates are thought to slow the accumulation of cellular damage at a temperature of 4.1 °C [T = 4.1 °C]. Age validation studies using bomb radiocarbon dating in otolith cores have confirmed that some individuals hatched in the 1940s were still present in the catch during the 2010s, attesting to the species' remarkable resilience to environmental variability. However, this same life-history strategy renders the Dusky rockfish particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, because the removal of older age classes can only be replaced over periods spanning multiple human generations, necessitating stringent harvest controls to maintain population stability.
